summary.text: The proof shows inductively that a cell at time \(t\ge1\) is off exactly when \(x=t-2v\) and \(\binom{t-1}{v}\) is odd, using Pascal’s identity to match the Rule 167 update. At the center this reduces, via Lucas parity, to \(t\) being a power of two—equivalently \(t\mid2^{t+1}\)—so appending the next middle-column bit gives the stated recurrence.

full_proof.text:
Let the state at time \(t\geq 0\) and position \(x\in\mathbb Z\) be denoted by \(C(t,x)\in\{0,1\}\). Initially,
\[
C(0,x)=\begin{cases}1,&x=0,\\0,&x\ne0.\end{cases}
\]
If the three entries at time \(t\) in positions \(x-1,x,x+1\) are \(L,C,R\), respectively, then Rule 167 defines the next entry to be the bit of \(167\) in position
\[
4L+2C+R,
\]
where the bit in position zero is the least significant bit. Since
\[
167=(10100111)_2,
\]
the outputs for indices \(0,1,\ldots,7\) are
\[
1,1,1,0,0,1,0,1.
\]
We shall use this truth table explicitly below.

Write
\[
b_t=C(t,0)
\]
for the middle-column bit at time \(t\). By the definition of the sequence,
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}b_j2^{n-j};
\]
thus \(a(n)\) is the integer whose binary expansion is the prefix
\(b_0b_1\cdots b_n\).

We first determine exactly which cells of the automaton are zero.

For \(t\geq1\), define the condition
\[
Z(t,x):\quad \text{there is a }v\geq0\text{ such that }x=t-2v
\text{ and }\binom{t-1}{v}\text{ is odd}.
\]
We claim that for every \(t\geq1\) and every \(x\in\mathbb Z\),
\[
C(t,x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Z(t,x),                    \tag{1}
\]
or equivalently,
\[
C(t,x)=\begin{cases}0,&Z(t,x),\\1,&\neg Z(t,x).\end{cases}       \tag{2}
\]

We prove this by induction on \(t\).

At time \(1\), the only zero is at \(x=1\). Indeed, at \(x=1\) the input triple is \((1,0,0)\), whose index is \(4\), and bit \(4\) of 167 is zero. At \(x=0\), \(x=-1\), and every other position, the triples are respectively \((0,1,0)\), \((0,0,1)\), and \((0,0,0)\), except that these descriptions already cover all positions touched by the initial 1; their indices are \(2,1,0\), and all three corresponding output bits are 1. On the other hand,
\[
Z(1,x)
\]
means that \(x=1-2v\) and \(\binom0v\) is odd. This happens only for \(v=0\), hence only for \(x=1\). Thus (1) holds at time 1.

Now suppose (2) holds at time \(s\), where \(s\geq1\), and consider a position \(x\) at time \(s+1\). There are two principal cases.

First suppose that
\[
x=s+1-2v                                                     \tag{3}
\]
for some \(v\geq0\). The position \(x\) itself has parity opposite to every integer of the form \(s-2w\). Consequently \(Z(s,x)\) is false, so the center input is
\[
C(s,x)=1.
\]

Assume initially that \(v\geq1\). Then
\[
x-1=s-2v,
\qquad
x+1=s-2(v-1).
\]
Hence, by the induction hypothesis, the left input is zero exactly when
\[
B:\quad \binom{s-1}{v}\text{ is odd},
\]
and the right input is zero exactly when
\[
A:\quad \binom{s-1}{v-1}\text{ is odd}.
\]
Pascal's identity gives
\[
\binom{s}{v}=\binom{s-1}{v-1}+\binom{s-1}{v}.                  \tag{4}
\]
Thus \(\binom{s}{v}\) is odd exactly when precisely one of \(A,B\) holds.

The four possibilities are now read directly from Rule 167:

* If neither \(A\) nor \(B\) holds, both neighbors are 1, so the input is \((1,1,1)\), of index 7, and the output is 1.
* If \(B\) holds but \(A\) does not, the input is \((0,1,1)\), of index 3, and the output is 0.
* If \(A\) holds but \(B\) does not, the input is \((1,1,0)\), of index 6, and the output is 0.
* If both \(A\) and \(B\) hold, the input is \((0,1,0)\), of index 2, and the output is 1.

Therefore the new cell is zero exactly when the sum on the right side of (4) is odd, that is, exactly when \(\binom{s}{v}\) is odd. In view of (3), this is precisely \(Z(s+1,x)\).

It remains within this first case to treat \(v=0\). Then \(x=s+1\). The left neighbor, at \(x-1=s\), satisfies \(Z(s,s)\), because it corresponds to the index \(0\) and \(\binom{s-1}{0}=1\). The right neighbor \(x+1=s+2\) cannot be of the form \(s-2w\) with \(w\geq0\), and, as noted above, the center does not satisfy \(Z(s,x)\). Thus the input is \((0,1,1)\), and Rule 167 gives output 0. This agrees with \(Z(s+1,s+1)\), since \(\binom{s}{0}=1\) is odd.

For the second principal case, suppose there is no \(v\geq0\) for which (3) holds. Then \(Z(s+1,x)\) is false. Moreover, neither neighbor can satisfy the old zero condition. Indeed, if
\[
x-1=s-2v,
\]
then \(x=s+1-2v\), contrary to the assumption; and if
\[
x+1=s-2v,
\]
then
\[
x=s+1-2(v+1),
\]
again a contradiction. Hence the left and right inputs are both 1. The center input may be either 0 or 1, but this does not matter: the two possible triples are \((1,0,1)\), of index 5, and \((1,1,1)\), of index 7, and Rule 167 outputs 1 in both cases. Thus the new cell is 1, exactly as required because \(Z(s+1,x)\) is false.

This completes the induction and proves (1).

We next specialize (1) to the middle column. For \(n\geq2\), the condition \(Z(n,0)\) says that for some \(v\geq0\),
\[
0=n-2v
\quad\text{and}\quad
\binom{n-1}{v}\text{ is odd}.
\]
The first equation is equivalent to \(n=2v\). Since \(n\geq2\), this forces \(v\geq1\), and therefore
\[
Z(n,0)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n=2v\text{ for some }v\geq1\text{ with } inom{2v-1}{v}\text{ odd}.       \tag{5}
\]

We now prove the needed parity characterization
\[
\binom{2v-1}{v}\text{ is odd}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v\text{ is a power of }2                                      \tag{6}
\]
for every \(v\geq1\).

We use the following elementary mod-2 form of Lucas's theorem. If
\[
N=2q+r,
\qquad
K=2\ell+e,
\qquad r,e\in\{0,1\},
\]
then
\[
\binom NK\equiv \binom re\binom q\ell\pmod2.                 \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, this follows by comparing coefficients in the polynomial ring over the field with two elements. There,
\[
(1+X)^{2q+r}=((1+X)^2)^q(1+X)^r=(1+X^2)^q(1+X)^r.
\]
The coefficient of \(X^{2\ell+e}\) is therefore the product of the coefficient \(\binom q\ell\) contributed by \((1+X^2)^q\) and the coefficient \(\binom re\) contributed by \((1+X)^r\), proving (7).

We also need the elementary fact
\[
\binom{2u}{u}\text{ is odd}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u=0.             \tag{8}
\]
For \(u=0\), the binomial coefficient is 1. If \(u\geq1\), Pascal's identity and symmetry give
\[
\binom{2u}{u}
 =\binom{2u-1}{u-1}+\binom{2u-1}{u}
 =2\binom{2u-1}{u},
\]
so it is even. This proves (8).

We prove (6) by strong induction on \(v\geq1\). Since
\[
2v-1=2(v-1)+1,
\]
formula (7) gives
\[
\binom{2v-1}{v}
\equiv
\binom{1}{v\bmod2}
\binom{v-1}{\lfloor v/2\rfloor}
\pmod2.                                                       \tag{9}
\]

If \(v=2u\) is even, then \(u\geq1\), and (9) reduces to
\[
\binom{2v-1}{v}
\equiv \binom{2u-1}{u}\pmod2.
\]
By the induction hypothesis, the expression on the right is odd exactly when \(u\) is a power of 2. But \(2u\) is a power of 2 exactly when \(u\) is, so (6) follows in the even case.

If \(v=2u+1\) is odd, (9) reduces to
\[
\binom{2v-1}{v}
\equiv \binom{2u}{u}\pmod2.
\]
By (8), this is odd exactly when \(u=0\), which is equivalent to \(v=1=2^0\). If \(u>0\), then \(v>1\) is odd and hence cannot be a power of 2. Thus (6) also follows in the odd case, completing the induction.

Combining (5) and (6), we find that, for \(n\geq2\), the center cell is zero exactly when
\[
n=2v\quad\text{with }v=2^k

after which
\[
n=2^{k+1}.
\]
Conversely, if \(n=2^j\geq2\), then \(j\geq1\); taking \(v=2^{j-1}\), condition (6) shows that \(Z(n,0)\) holds. Hence
\[
C(n,0)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\text{ is a power of }2                                     \tag{10}
\]
for every \(n\geq2\).

We relate this to the arithmetic condition in the conjecture. For every positive integer \(n\),
\[
n\mid 2^{n+1}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\text{ is a power of }2.                                    \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, every divisor of a power of the prime 2 has no prime divisor other than 2, and is therefore itself \(2^k\) for some \(k\geq0\). Conversely, if \(n=2^k\), then \(k\leq 2^k+1=n+1\) (for example, the standard induction gives \(k<2^k\)), so
\[
2^k\mid 2^{n+1}.
\]
Thus (11) holds.

Now let
\[
r=2^{n+1}\bmod n.
\]
Because \(n\geq2\), we have
\[
r=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\mid2^{n+1}.               \tag{12}
\]
Also, since \(r\) is a nonnegative integer,
\[
\left\lfloor\left(\frac12\right)^r\right\rfloor
=
\begin{cases}
1,&r=0,\\
0,&r>0.
\end{cases}                                                   \tag{13}
\]
Indeed, the value is 1 when \(r=0\), while it lies strictly between 0 and 1 when \(r>0\).

Let
\[
F(n)=\left\lfloor\left(\frac12\right)^{(2^{n+1}\bmod n)}\right\rfloor.
\]
Equations (10)--(13) show that, for every \(n\geq2\),
\[
F(n)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\mid2^{n+1}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\text{ is a power of }2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
C(n,0)=0.
\]
Both \(F(n)\) and \(C(n,0)\) are either 0 or 1. Therefore
\[
b_n=C(n,0)=1-F(n).                                           \tag{14}
\]

It remains only to convert this bit formula into the claimed recurrence for the binary-prefix values. From the definition of \(a(n)\), for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
&=\sum_{j=0}^{n}b_j2^{n-j}\\
&=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}b_j2^{n-j}+b_n\\
&=2\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}b_j2^{(n-1)-j}+b_n\\
&=2a(n-1)+b_n.
\end{aligned}                                                 \tag{15}
\]
Finally, for \(n\geq2\), substitute (14) into (15). This gives
\[
\boxed{
 a(n)=2a(n-1)+1-
 \left\lfloor\left(\frac12\right)^{(2^{n+1}\bmod n)}\right\rfloor
}.
\]
Since the floor term is always either 0 or 1, the displayed subtraction is nonnegative and agrees with ordinary integer subtraction. This proves the conjectured recurrence for every integer \(n\geq2\).
